items.prompt: What is the passage’s central concern?
options: Every negative result proves that a treatment is useless
Selective reporting can distort the overall evidence about a treatment
Only successful experiments need methodological descriptions
Unpublished research always involves dishonest measurements
items.explanation: The text examines how visibility affects the combined evidence.
items.title: The Value of a Negative Result
items.passage:
An experiment that finds no effect can be difficult to publish. Researchers and readers may be more interested in a new treatment that produces an improvement than in one that appears to do nothing. Yet overlooking negative results can distort the evidence available for making decisions.
Suppose several teams test the same treatment. If only the successful experiments become widely visible, a later reviewer may conclude that the treatment is more dependable than the full set of experiments would suggest. The problem is not necessarily dishonesty within any individual report. It can arise from the selective visibility of findings across many reports.
Publishing every unsuccessful experiment without evaluation is not a solution. A study may be too small to detect an important effect or may use an unsuitable measure. Readers need enough methodological information to interpret what the absence of a detected effect actually means. A well-designed negative study can rule out some possibilities, while a weak one may leave the question open.
Some research systems address selective reporting by recording study plans before results are known. Such records make it easier to identify completed studies that were never published. The aim is not to treat all findings as equally informative, but to prevent the direction of a result from being the main reason it enters the shared body of evidence.

items.prompt: What does the passage argue about pictures in instructions?
options: Their meaning is identical for every reader
They are useful only after an assembly has failed
They are useful for some information but must be designed and tested carefully
They always make written explanations unnecessary
items.explanation: The text balances spatial benefits against ambiguity and user needs.
items.title: Why Some Instructions Use Pictures
items.passage:
Instructions for assembling an object often combine words with diagrams. A diagram can show the relative positions of parts more directly than a long verbal description. This does not mean that pictures are universally easier to understand. Their usefulness depends on what information the task requires and what the reader can interpret.
An unfamiliar symbol can create uncertainty. A curved arrow might mean that a component should rotate, but a reader may not know whether the rotation applies to the whole assembly or one small part. Designers can reduce ambiguity by showing an intermediate state or labeling the relevant component.
Testing instructions with users frequently reveals difficulties that experts overlook. Someone who already knows how an object fits together may mentally supply a missing step. A novice cannot necessarily make the same inference. Asking users to explain what they intend to do before they act can expose a misunderstanding without waiting for the object to be assembled incorrectly.
Effective instructions therefore use representations strategically. Words may be better for stating a condition or warning, while diagrams clarify spatial relationships. The goal is not to minimize the number of words at any cost. It is to coordinate the available forms of information so that a reader can carry out the required action accurately and safely.

lower.prompt: Why might opening at a characteristic time benefit a flowering plant?
options: It ensures that every visiting animal pollinates it

It prevents the flower from ever closing

lower.explanation: The first paragraph identifies contact with active pollinators.
lower.title: A Clock in a Flower
lower.passage:
Many flowering plants open their flowers at characteristic times of day. This pattern may bring flowers into contact with pollinators when those animals are most active. It can also help protect delicate structures during less favorable conditions. The visible opening is the result of interacting biological and environmental processes.
Some plants respond directly to changes in light or temperature. Others also show an internal daily rhythm. Researchers can distinguish these influences by keeping plants under controlled conditions. If a pattern continues for a time without the usual daily changes in light, an internal timing mechanism is likely to contribute.
An internal rhythm is not entirely independent of the environment. Natural light cycles can synchronize it with local conditions. A plant moved into a different schedule may gradually shift its activity rather than changing instantly. The time required for adjustment gives researchers information about how environmental cues and internal processes interact.
These observations caution against interpreting a flower’s schedule as a simple reaction to the current weather. A flower opening on a cloudy morning may still reflect a rhythm established by earlier cycles. At the same time, internal timing does not make immediate conditions irrelevant. Both inherited timing systems and present conditions can influence when a flower is available to a visiting pollinator.

higher.prompt: What is the main argument?
options: A map is useful only if every distance is represented precisely
A map’s simplifications should be understood in relation to its purpose
Every distortion indicates careless mapmaking
Digital maps eliminate decisions about selection
higher.explanation: Purpose explains selection and the limits of inference.
higher.title: Choosing What a Map Leaves Out
higher.passage:
A map is useful partly because it leaves information out. A drawing that attempted to include every feature at its original size would be as difficult to navigate as the landscape itself. Mapmakers choose which relationships to emphasize according to the task the map is meant to support.
A transit diagram offers a familiar example. It may show stations at roughly equal intervals even when the actual distances between them differ greatly. The diagram helps passengers identify connections and the order of stops, but it may be unsuitable for estimating how far they must walk above ground. The distortion is purposeful rather than necessarily a mistake.
The same principle applies to thematic maps, which emphasize a particular kind of information. A map of rainfall can group measurements into shaded categories. The boundaries between categories simplify a continuous pattern, and the selected ranges influence how large differences appear. A reader should therefore examine the legend instead of treating every change in shading as an equally large change in the underlying measurements.
Digital maps can reveal additional layers on demand, yet they still involve selection. Screen size, scale and visual priority affect what is readily visible. Good map reading involves asking both what a map shows clearly and what its design makes difficult to infer.

higher.passage:
A map is useful partly because it leaves information out. A drawing that attempted to include every feature at its original size would be as difficult to navigate as the landscape itself. Mapmakers choose which relationships to emphasize according to the task the map is meant to support.
A transit diagram offers a familiar example. It may show stations at roughly equal intervals even when the actual distances between them differ greatly. The distortion is purposeful rather than necessarily a mistake.
The same principle applies to thematic maps, which emphasize a particular kind of information. A map of rainfall can group measurements into shaded categories. The boundaries between categories simplify a continuous pattern, and the selected ranges influence how large differences appear. A reader should therefore examine the legend instead of treating every change in shading as an equally large change in the underlying measurements.

stimulus.title: A Museum Object without a Name
stimulus.script:
Sometimes a museum holds an object whose maker or original owner is unknown. That does not mean the object has nothing to tell us. Its material, wear and relationship to other objects can support questions about use and production, even when a personal name cannot be recovered.
Wear marks offer one kind of clue. Repeated contact can polish an edge or leave scratches in a particular direction. Researchers compare these marks with examples produced experimentally or with objects of known use. A resemblance can support an interpretation, but several different activities may leave similar traces. Conclusions should reflect that uncertainty.
Collection history is another source. A note written when an object entered a museum might identify where it was found. Yet older records can be incomplete or shaped by assumptions that later research questions. The record itself must be evaluated rather than treated as automatically correct.
Museums can communicate these distinctions to visitors. A label may explain what is known, what is inferred and what remains unknown. This can be more educational than presenting an uncertain story with unjustified confidence. An incomplete history is not a reason to stop investigating; it is a reason to make the basis and limits of an interpretation visible.

stimulus.title: An Experiment in Listening
stimulus.script:
A researcher plays two tones and asks listeners whether they are different. The task seems simple, but the instruction can influence how people respond. Some listeners may report a difference whenever they are slightly uncertain, while others may answer differently unless they are very sure.
This means that a response can reflect both sensitivity to the sounds and a decision strategy. Researchers often include trials in which the tones are identical. If someone frequently reports differences on those trials, the pattern helps interpret their answers on genuinely different pairs. Counting correct answers alone may miss this distinction.
Practice and feedback can change the strategy as well as the ability being measured. A participant who believes that differences are extremely rare may become reluctant to report one. Experimenters therefore describe the procedure consistently and examine several kinds of response, rather than relying on one total.
The same general issue appears in other detection tasks, such as noticing a visual signal or identifying a faint event in a recording. A useful experiment asks not only whether a person responded correctly but how the conditions encouraged them to make a decision. That distinction helps avoid attributing every change in performance to a change in perception itself.

stimulus.title: The Life of a Temporary Exhibition
stimulus.script:
Temporary exhibitions are often planned around a public opening date. Behind that date is a sequence of interdependent tasks: borrowing objects, checking their condition, designing cases and preparing interpretation. A delay in one part can affect several others, even when it seems minor on its own.
For example, a display designer needs reliable dimensions before constructing a support. If an object arrives later than expected, measurements supplied in advance become especially important. Yet a measurement alone may not reveal a fragile surface that requires a different support. Communication between lenders, conservators and designers helps resolve such issues.
Text preparation has a similar dependency. A label cannot simply be written at the last moment if it needs editing, translation or accessibility review. Scheduling these steps early can reduce rushed decisions near installation. The goal is not to prevent every revision but to make necessary revisions possible without sacrificing essential checks.
After the exhibition closes, the work continues. Borrowed objects need condition checks and safe return arrangements, while evaluation can inform future projects. Thinking of an exhibition as a process rather than only a finished room makes this less visible work easier to understand. The opening is a significant milestone, but it is neither the beginning nor the end of the whole undertaking.

stimulus.title: When a Useful Comparison Fails
stimulus.script:
Comparing two places can help explain a pattern, but a comparison is only as useful as the reasoning behind it. Suppose one neighborhood has more street trees and lower summer temperatures than another. The difference is consistent with a cooling effect, but it does not isolate that effect automatically.
The neighborhoods may also differ in building height, distance from water or the amount of paved ground. Those features could influence temperature too. Researchers try to measure relevant differences and, where possible, compare locations that are similar in other respects. They may also follow the same locations over time as conditions change.
No approach removes every uncertainty. A neighborhood is not a laboratory chamber where each factor can be adjusted independently. That limitation does not make investigation pointless. It means that evidence from several approaches can be more informative than a single striking contrast.
The important habit is to ask what else could produce the observed difference and what evidence would help separate the explanations. A photograph of a cool, leafy street beside a hot, bare one can communicate a plausible idea, but a persuasive explanation requires more than choosing two examples that fit it.
